strengths: Addresses timely and practically important problem: emergent misalignment poses real security risks for fine-tuning APIs
Thoughtful evaluation framework measuring both EMA mitigation and benign task performance, capturing key practical trade-offs
Systematic empirical evaluation with comprehensive hyperparameter ablations across multiple model sizes and datasets
Clear presentation of method trade-offs; honest discussion of limitations (e.g., KL-divergence inhibiting benign task learning, interleaving introducing incoherence)
Strong reproducibility focus with detailed hyperparameters, promised code release, and methodological transparency
Measures both out-of-domain (EMA) and in-domain misaligned task performance, providing nuanced understanding of what is actually suppressed
weaknesses: No novel methodological contributions: paper evaluates existing methods without proposing new approaches or solutions to the documented problems
Narrow evaluation scope: only 4 EMA datasets (all synthetic/LLM-filtered), only 1 realistic benign task (FoQA), limited to Qwen2.5 models. Generalization across architectures and domains unclear

Evaluation methodology compromises: uses GPT-4o-mini instead of GPT-4o for alignment judgment; arbitrary thresholds for misalignment (alignment < 30, coherence > 50) without sensitivity analysis; small sample sizes for in-domain evaluation (30 questions)
Lacks mechanistic understanding: why does LDIFS fail? Why does KL-divergence succeed on FoQA but completely fail on OpSwap? These critical questions remain unanswered beyond 'it's an open question'
Incoherence trade-off inadequately explored: interleaving shows 34% higher incoherence on Security dataset but is treated as secondary concern; no granular analysis of incoherence types
Dramatic in-domain learning failure of KL-divergence (only 42-46% of baseline) raises practical concerns for practitioners but is insufficiently analyzed

Missing mechanistic insights and comparisons: limited direct comparison with contemporaneous work (Wang et al. achieve ~85% via SAE steering); no exploration of combining methods or adaptive approaches
OpSwap task is highly synthetic with limited real-world relevance; the contradiction between OpSwap and FoQA results deserves deeper investigation
Essentially a negative results paper documenting that current methods are inadequate, without providing solutions or deep insights into why

strengths: Well-motivated problem with timely safety relevance for fine-tuning APIs
Thoughtful evaluation framework that captures important trade-offs between EMA mitigation and benign task performance
Honest and transparent reporting of negative results, limitations, and trade-offs without overselling findings
Comprehensive empirical details with extensive hyperparameter ablations and clear documentation supporting reproducibility
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1 clearly illustrates desired vs. current state gap)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily an empirical evaluation of existing methods (KL-div from 2017, LDIFS/SafeLoRA/interleaving from prior work) rather than novel approaches or mechanisms
Negative results without compelling alternatives: concludes current methods are insufficient but lacks strong new directions or practical guidance for practitioners
Narrow experimental scope for top-tier venue: only 2 model sizes (both Qwen), 4 EMA tasks, and 2 benign tasks; unclear generalization to broader settings or larger models where EMA is stronger

Questionable benign task selection: OpSwap is artificial; FoQA is low-resource language QA where models lack prior knowledge, and KL-divergence actually improves on FoQA (+3%), contradicting OpSwap findings and suggesting task-specificity rather than fundamental limitation
Evaluation methodology concerns: GPT-4o-mini substitution not validated, misalignment threshold (< 30 alignment AND > 50 coherence) appears arbitrary without sensitivity analysis

Severe hyperparameter sensitivity without practical guidance: Figure 2 shows steep trade-offs between EMA reduction and coherence with no principled framework for practitioners to select hyperparameters for their use case

Incomplete exploration of interleaving: dismisses in-domain safe data (shown more effective in Wang et al. 2025) without empirical comparison; unclear why general-domain WildGuardMix was chosen over in-domain alternatives
Unexplained null result: LDIFS completely ineffective (3.64 vs 4.01 baseline) deserves investigation but receives minimal discussion
Reproducibility gaps: code URL stated as missing in manuscript; LLM-as-judge evaluation depends on GPT-4o-mini which may drift; only tested on specific Qwen models

Limited discussion of why results may not generalize: paper acknowledges 'open question how much KL-divergence impacts real-world tasks in practice' but this undermines a key claim about learning inhibition

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem in LLM safety with clear motivation for API providers
Rigorous experimental design with systematic evaluation across multiple EMA-inducing domains and measurement of both narrow and broad misalignment
Thoughtful characterization of trade-offs between EMA mitigation and benign task performance, demonstrating that none of the methods are fully satisfactory
Comprehensive hyperparameter ablations and reproducibility details (code release, full hyperparameters, compute requirements)
Honest reporting of negative results without overstating findings; valuable for guiding future research directions
Clear presentation and effective visualizations, particularly the problem framing in Figure 1
First systematic study of in-training defenses against EMA, establishing baseline understanding of existing approaches
weaknesses: Limited scope of benign task evaluation: only two tasks (one synthetic OpSwap, one real FoQA); additional real-world tasks would better characterize the methods' impact on practical use cases
Evaluation heavily dependent on LLM-as-judge scoring with arbitrary thresholds (alignment < 30, coherence > 50); limited to 30 questions per dataset for in-domain evaluation
Limited model scope: only Qwen2.5 tested; generalization to GPT, Llama, or Claude architectures unclear; only LoRA fine-tuning evaluated

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: paper documents what works but provides limited insight into why trade-offs occur (e.g., why KL-divergence prevents task learning, why interleaving increases incoherence)
All four methods are existing techniques applied to a new problem; no novel mitigation methods or theoretical advances in understanding EMA mechanisms proposed
Limited practical impact: conclusions show current methods are insufficient without providing clear solutions for practitioners

Synthetic dataset creation for Legal/Medical/Security domains may not represent real fine-tuning failures; no exploration of method combinations or modified approaches to address identified trade-offs

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem—emergent misalignment in fine-tuned LLMs—with direct relevance to deployed systems offering API fine-tuning

Comprehensive multi-dimensional empirical evaluation across four EMA domains (Code, Legal, Medical, Security) and three benign tasks, examining EMA mitigation, narrow misalignment retention, benign learning, and coherence simultaneously
Systematic hyperparameter ablations (Appendix B.1-B.3) clearly demonstrating trade-offs between metrics, providing valuable guidance for practitioners on method selection
Honest and thorough limitations discussion, acknowledging reliance on GPT-4o-mini judges, limited benign task breadth, and restricted RL evaluation rather than overselling results
Strong reproducibility practices including promised code release, detailed hyperparameters, open-source base models, and ablation studies across model sizes (7B and 32B)
Proposes Interleaving++ as a practical, low-cost intervention (5% overhead) that balances multiple competing objectives better than existing methods
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Interleaving++ is a straightforward application of Moore & Lewis (2010)'s existing data selection technique; core methods (KL-div, LDIFS, Persona Vectors, Interleaving) are all prior work

Heavy evaluation reliance on GPT-4o-mini LLM judges without sufficient validation—claims of 'qualitative stability' when re-running with GPT-4o lack supporting evidence of absolute score shifts; known issues with LLM judges regarding demographic and cultural bias
Small EMA evaluation set (24 questions from single source) raises questions about robustness of conclusions; binary coherence threshold (< 50) appears coarse and lacks justification

Lacks theoretical or mechanistic insight into why methods succeed/fail: no explanation for KL-divergence's OpSwap failure versus FoQA success, Persona Vector RL collapse, or why perplexity gap predicts useful training data

Limited benign task evaluation (acknowledged by authors as compute-constrained): OpSwap synthetic, FoQA domain-specific low-resource QA, GSM8K math-only; missing standard NLU benchmarks, diverse instruction-following, and real-world applications

Computational cost of Interleaving++ inadequately addressed: requires training K misaligned models for perplexity computation, with no clear quantification of overhead; design choice to filter refusals appears ad-hoc and potentially method-specific
RL evaluation severely limited: single task (GSM8K), one epoch, high variance (±10%), relegates dramatic Persona Vector failure to brief mention without investigation

Improvements over simple Interleaving baseline often modest (e.g., Code EMA 0.58→0.30) with persistent trade-offs; claim that Interleaving++ 'works well in all settings' overstated given higher incoherence than Persona Vectors on some datasets
Data selection scoring (Eq. 6) lacks justification: choice of averaging K misaligned model losses, ε regularization, and relative gap metric are pragmatic but not theoretically motivated
Generalization concerns: evaluation only on Qwen models; EMA originally demonstrated on larger models (GPT-4o); applicability to other architectures and different EMA manifestations unclear

strengths: Addresses timely and practically relevant problem of emergent misalignment in API fine-tuning scenarios

Comprehensive systematic evaluation across four methods and four evaluation dimensions (EMA prevention, narrow misalignment learning, benign task performance, coherence) with thorough hyperparameter ablations
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations including evaluation judge quality, scale constraints, synthetic stress-test scenarios, and dual-use risks
Multi-faceted evaluation design appropriately avoids solutions that simply disable learning
Well-motivated benign task selection (e.g., FoQA for testing realistic low-resource scenarios)
Strong reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, extensive appendices, and promised code release
weaknesses: Severe scale mismatch: all experiments on Qwen2.5-7B/32B while EMA is most pronounced in GPT-4o-scale models; claims about 'practical methods for providers' lack validation where the problem matters most

Questionable evaluation methodology: relies on GPT-4o-mini instead of GPT-4o (cost-driven downgrade); only 24 open-ended questions; LLM-as-judge is known to have cultural biases and systematic blindspots; arbitrary thresholds (alignment <30, coherence >50)

Limited benign task evaluation: OpSwap is a synthetic stress-test specifically designed to break KL; only one realistic task (FoQA); no standard NLU benchmarks; RL evaluation on single task with 3B model only
Datasets are partly synthetic and LLM-generated with potential normative biases; real-world misalignment patterns likely differ significantly from synthetic stress-tests

All methods exhibit serious failure modes with no clear winner: KL fails on OpSwap tiers (0-1% vs 30-40%), Persona Vectors catastrophically fails in RL (reduces to 0-38% accuracy), LDIFS ineffective, Interleaving++ only method showing balance

Interleaving++ relies on ad-hoc design choices: requires K separately trained misaligned models (operationally expensive and unclear), brittle refusal heuristic (first 10 words), perplexity gap selection is not novel (Moore & Lewis 2010)

Limited mechanistic understanding: paper doesn't explain why perplexity gap selection outperforms random sampling, why LDIFS fails despite targeting concept preservation, or deeper insights into method differences

Unrealistic threat model: all experiments on 'stress-test regimes designed to probe failure modes'; unclear if real customers intentionally fine-tune on misaligned data; generalization to actual deployment scenarios questionable
Strong hyperparameter sensitivity throughout (Figure 1b) undermines robustness claims; chosen hyperparameters appear somewhat arbitrary rather than principled
No statistical significance testing; most results lack confidence intervals; some differences between methods could be within noise
RL evaluation insufficient: only GSM8K, single model size, persona vector catastrophic failure not thoroughly investigated, SFT/RL batch ratio sensitivity unclear
Practical deployment path unclear: Interleaving++ operationally expensive, K selection strategy not discussed, computational overhead not quantified
Dual-use concerns not fully mitigated: perplexity gap technique could be reversed for attacks; 'responsible disclosure' remains vague

strengths: Addresses an important and timely safety problem (emergent misalignment) with high practical relevance for API model providers
First systematic study of in-training defenses against EMA, providing comprehensive comparison across multiple methods (KL-divergence, LDIFS, persona vectors, interleaving)
Proposes practical solution (Interleaving++) achieving ~95% EMA reduction with only 5% computational overhead, making it readily deployable
Comprehensive and well-designed experimental evaluation across 4 EMA datasets, 3 benign datasets, multiple metrics, both SFT and RL settings, with careful hyperparameter ablations
Maintains performance on benign tasks and in-domain misalignment—key requirement for a practical defense
Sound methodology with clear trade-offs identified between methods; results validated on both 7B and 32B models
Honest and thorough limitations discussion acknowledging constraints (model scale, compute budget, LLM-as-judge reliance, synthetic datasets)
Clear presentation with effective use of tables and figures to communicate complex multi-metric results; code promised for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing methods (KL-divergence, LDIFS, persona vectors) and adapts existing data selection technique (Moore & Lewis 2010) without significant algorithmic innovation
Evaluation constrained to smaller models (7B, 32B) due to cost; unclear generalization to frontier models where EMA is most robust and concerning for API providers
Incomplete benign task evaluation due to compute constraints (only 3 datasets); FoQA results show unexpected improvements with KL and persona vectors (Table 4) that deserve investigation
Heavy reliance on LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o-mini) for evaluation of safety-critical behaviors; limited human evaluation despite critical importance of alignment/coherence assessment
RL evaluation severely limited to single task (GSM8K); persona vectors show catastrophic failure in RL (Table 5) but mechanism unexplored—critical limitation given increasing RL fine-tuning adoption
All methods highly sensitive to hyperparameters (Figure 1b); limited guidance for practitioners on selecting hyperparameters for new fine-tuning tasks without access to misaligned models
Synthetic EMA datasets may not capture real-world fine-tuning failure modes; datasets generated and filtered using LLMs which can encode generating model biases
Limited mechanistic insight: why perplexity gap selection outperforms random sampling unexplained; what properties of selected data matter; how method scales with safety data amount
Missing analysis of why KL-divergence completely blocks learning for higher OpSwap tiers (Table 3) and why persona vectors fail catastrophically in RL
Persona vector approach reliable for SFT but fails for RL, limiting reliability for providers supporting multiple fine-tuning modalities; no clear path to fixing this
